intro: Brno pulled down its city walls between 1809 and 1859 and planted a ring of parks where they had stood. Seven protected trees grow in and around that ring: two oaks at opposite ends of one square, a horse chestnut opposite the opera house, a plane on the ramparts below the cathedral, another on hospital ground, one renamed for a professor, and the thickest on a corner where a bus station used to be. The eighth and oldest is out in Bystrc, a lime past four hundred years that somebody once tried to burn a marten out of.
meta_description: Brno's protected trees: a 400-year-old lime that survived a fire lit to drive out a marten, two oaks on Moravske namesti, and a 5.7-metre plane.
question_meta: Brno's oldest tree is likely the oak at the south end of Moravske namesti, given as over 170 years. Where it stands, and what else is on the walk.
question_answer: Brno's oldest tree is the lime on náměstí 28. dubna in Bystrc, put at 380 to 400 years old around the year 2000, so somewhere past four centuries now. It is a long way ahead of everything else on this page. The next oldest is The Old Town Gate Oak at the southern entrance to the Moravské náměstí park, which the city's own heritage encyclopedia records as more than 170 years old, followed by a horse chestnut and a plane at around 160 years and the plane at St Anne's hospital at over 150. Every one of those figures is an estimate. The Czech national register of memorial trees gives each tree a code, a species, a girth, a height and a position, and it has no age field at all, so the ages here come from city and tourism sources rather than from measurement. The plane on the corner of Benešova has no published age at all, which is why this page gives it none.
question_context: Brno's protected trees are documented twice over, which is why this page can be specific about trunks and vague about years. The Czech national register of memorial trees, kept by the AOPK, gives each a code, a species, a girth, a height and a position, several last updated in 2024, but no age. Local sources fill part of that gap with estimates and older measurements, which is why several girths appear as a range: the tape went round different trunks in different decades, or two sources simply disagree, as they do for the plane renamed after Professor Chudoba. Seven of the eight stand within about 1.1 kilometres of each other in and around the ring of parks laid out where the fortifications came down. The eighth, the lime in Bystrc, is a separate trip 7 km northwest, and it is both the oldest tree here and the best documented. Two others carry a caveat: the plane at St Anne's stands on a working hospital campus, and the oak at the south end of Moravské náměstí has not been photographed by anyone we could find since 2015.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Brno?
faq.a: The lime on náměstí 28. dubna in Bystrc, estimated at 380 to 400 years old around the year 2000. The Czech memorial-tree register carries no age field, so that figure is an estimate rather than a measurement. In the centre, the oldest is the oak at the southern entrance to the Moravské náměstí park, recorded by Brno's heritage encyclopedia as over 170 years old.

faq.q: Are Brno's memorial trees free to visit?
faq.a: All eight, and none of them needs a ticket. Two need a word of warning. The plane at St Anne's grows on the grounds of a working teaching hospital, reached through the gate on the south side off Hybešova, and the little terrace holding the plane below Petrov is planted up for the tourist season and closed off in winter, when you look at it from the path instead.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Seven of them, yes. The furthest two of those are about 1.1 kilometres apart, Benešova at one end and St Anne's at the other, with everything else in between, and Professor Chudoba's plane on Veveří does not stretch the walk further. Allow an hour and a half if you stop at each. The lime in Bystrc is 7 km out and is its own trip, about 25 minutes on the bus.

faq.q: What does 'memorial tree' mean in the Czech Republic?
faq.a: Památný strom is a legal status, not a nickname. A tree gets it for its size, age, appearance or history, and with it comes a protection zone around the trunk in which nothing may be done that would damage the tree. The oak at the south end of Moravské náměstí has a zone of 13.4 metres in every direction.

trees.name: The Moravian Square Oak

location.address: Moravské náměstí (park), near the fountain, Brno-střed

trees.story: Brno put a price on this oak before it protected it: more than 600,000 Kčs, the figure on record when the city's national committee declared it a memorial tree on 27 June 1985, alongside two other trees in the same park. The reason given was plain enough. It was the strongest tree there, and a solitary specimen worth keeping. The park is a piece of demolition. Brno pulled down its city walls between 1809 and 1859 and laid a ring of green where the fortifications had run, and Moravské náměstí is one link in that ring. At roughly 150 years, the oak is about as old as the planting around it. Today it stands just under 30 metres, with a trunk of 435 to 440 centimetres depending on which year you take the tape from: the city's figure and the national register's differ by five centimetres and a few seasons of growth, not by any real disagreement. Around 2005 arborists took out its dead wood, and it has been reported in good health since. Czech signs call it Dub letní na Moravském náměstí. Turistika.cz calls it the most beautiful memorial oak in Brno, which is a strong claim in a park that holds a second protected oak 130 metres down the grass.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak in the upper part of the park, near the fountain. A second protected oak of the same species stands 130 metres south at the far tip of the park, so go by which end you are standing at.

trees.name: The Old Town Gate Oak

location.address: Moravské náměstí (south end of the park), Brno-střed

trees.story: The law draws a circle round this oak. It runs 13.4 metres from the trunk in every direction, and inside it nothing may be done that would harm the tree, which is a generous amount of ground to fence off with a regulation in the middle of a city. The oak stands at the southern tip of the Moravské náměstí park, close to where the Tišnovská brána, the Tišnov Gate, once let travellers through Brno's walls. The gate is gone. So are the walls, taken down between 1809 and 1859 and replaced by the ring of parks the tree now grows in. Its measurements come from different decades and it shows. Brno's heritage encyclopedia recorded 410 centimetres round in 2004 and 423 in 2010; the national register carries 480, from a record last touched in 2018. Height is about 25 metres, and the age is given as more than 170 years, which is as precise as anyone has been willing to be. One honest note. The freshest photograph we could find of this particular oak, rather than of its better known neighbour 130 metres north, was taken in May 2015, and the register still lists it as standing. If you get there before we do, tell us what you found.
trees.how_to_recognise: At the southern tip of the park, the end nearest the tram tracks. The other protected oak is 130 metres north, up near the fountain.
verified_sources: AOPK CR pamatne stromy register (data/registers/czech-aopk-pamatne-stromy.json, kod 106252, CC BY 4.0)

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Rooseveltova

location.address: Park Danuše Muzikářové, Rooseveltova, opposite the Janáček Theatre

trees.story: A car park nearly wrote the end of this chestnut's story. When plans came up for an underground garage beneath the little park on Rooseveltova, the architecture press covered them as a question about one tree: whether digging that close to a protected trunk would take its roots with it. The tree is a horse chestnut of about 160 years, protected since 2007, standing in the middle of the park opposite the Janáček Theatre and a short walk from the old Governor's Palace. It survives from the first redesign of this ground after Brno's fortifications came down, when a strip that had carried walls became gardens instead. Its trunk measures between 320 and 326 centimetres at chest height, two numbers from different surveys rather than two different trees, and it stands about 25 metres tall. In 2019 the park around it was renamed Park Danuše Muzikářové. The tree kept its own name, Jírovec maďal na Rooseveltově, and its own quiet job in the city's year: in May it is the flowering tree in a square full of theatre-goers, and by late September the ground beneath it is a conker supply for anyone who wants one.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles open right across the crown

trees.name: The Plane Tree Below Petrov

location.address: Terrace on the old ramparts, end of Denisovy sady park, below Petrov Cathedral

trees.story: One of Brno's protected trees keeps seasonal hours. The plane below Petrov grows on a small terrace built into the old city ramparts at the end of Denisovy sady, and that terrace is planted up with flower displays through the tourist season and closed off in winter. Come in January and you look at the tree from the path instead of standing under it, which is worth knowing before you walk up the hill. The plane is about 160 years old, its crown reaching some 25 metres, and its trunk measures 400 to 415 centimetres depending on whose tape and which year: the national register carries the lower figure, turistika.cz the higher one. Above it stands the Cathedral of St Peter and Paul, the silhouette in every photograph of the city. Denisovy sady itself was laid out along the ramparts, which makes this corner one of the few places in Brno where the defensive works survive as landscape rather than as a line on a map. The Czech name is Platan javorolistý na Petrově. Locals will tell you this is the best corner of the park, and standing on the terrace with the rooftops in front of you and the cathedral at your back, it is hard to argue.

trees.transport: Roughly 10 minutes on foot from Brno hlavní nádraží (the main train station); inside Denisovy sady, near Zelný trh (the Cabbage Market)
trees.notes: Register kod 101080, isop_id 44660, also called Platan pod Petrovem. Girth 415cm per turistika.cz against 400cm in the register. Wikimedia Commons holds photographs of this tree uploaded February 2026.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of St Anne's

location.address: Grounds of St Anne's University Hospital (Fakultní nemocnice u sv. Anny), Pekařská, between pavilions V and C1

trees.story: The biggest tree on this walk is not in a park. It grows on the grounds of St Anne's University Hospital between pavilions V and C1, and the easiest way in is the gate on the south side off Hybešova. Nobody asks your business at a public teaching hospital, but this is a working campus rather than a public garden, so take it quietly. The plane repays the detour. Its trunk measures 565 to 575 centimetres round, the two figures a few years apart rather than two different trees, and it divides into several secondary stems about four metres up. Before the crown was cut back it spread close to 40 metres, measured in 2004. The hospital behind it went up between 1865 and 1868, a Neo-Renaissance design by the Viennese architect Theophil Hansen. Local sources suspect the tree was planted with the building, which would put it over 150 years old, but nobody has demonstrated that and the register carries no age at all, so treat the link as likely rather than settled. What is certain is that this crown has been the view from a great many hospital windows, in a city that has been sending its sick to this address for more than a century and a half.
trees.how_to_recognise: Between pavilions V and C1, and obvious once you are in the right courtyard: nothing else on the campus comes close to a trunk of five and a half metres round.
verified_sources: AOPK CR pamatne stromy register (data/registers/czech-aopk-pamatne-stromy.json, kod 101082, CC BY 4.0)
trees.access: On the grounds of St Anne's University Hospital, a public teaching hospital, not a private clinic. Enter through the gate on the south side off Hybešova; the campus is open on foot during the day and nobody asks your business, but this is hospital ground rather than a park
trees.transport: Roughly 15-20 minutes on foot from Brno hlavní nádraží (the main train station), or a short walk from the Mendlovo náměstí tram and bus interchange
trees.notes: Register kod 101082, isop_id 44662. Species recorded in the source as Platanus x hispanica, normalised to the site's canonical Platanus x acerifolia (same hybrid, hard rule 9). Girth 565cm per turistika.cz against 575cm in the register. Canopy reached almost 40m before the crown was trimmed, measured 2004. Flagged because this is hospital-campus land rather than a park, stated plainly in the access line and in the story.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Benešova

location.address: Corner of Benešova and Divadelní streets, by the site of the former Brno bus station
location.neighbourhood: Brno-střed (city centre, near the main train station)

trees.story: This plane outlasted a bus station. The corner of Benešova and Divadelní held Brno's central bus terminal, a modernist building of 1948 and 1949 by Bohuslav Fuchs, a name attached to much of the city's functionalist architecture. The buses left. The tree stayed, and it is now the protected thing on a corner where everything else has changed its use at least once. It is the plainest entry on this walk, not a park specimen but a street tree at a junction five minutes from the main station, which is exactly what makes it easy to find. Its trunk measures 368 centimetres in the national register; the Czech Wikipedia list of the district's memorial trees gives 310 at the same coordinates, an older measurement rather than a different tree. Nobody has published an age for it, anywhere, and that gap stays a gap here rather than becoming a plausible number. Brno's own street records list the tree as Benešova 0/01, a plot rather than a building, which is what Czech addressing does with something that has been given standing of its own. Walk past it on the way in from the train and you have started this walk before you meant to.

trees.access: Free, public street corner and pavement
trees.transport: Roughly 5 minutes on foot from Brno hlavní nádraží (the main train station)

trees.name: Professor Chudoba's Plane

location.address: Corner of Veveří and Pekárenská streets, Brno-Veveří

trees.story:
A professor put this tree on the record by complaining about everything around it. František Chudoba, Masaryk University's first professor of English philology, walked past this corner every day on his way to teach, and in a 1930 newspaper column he tore into Brno's neglected public greenery, then singled out this one plane tree as proof that something could still thrive here despite the city's indifference. The plane took the compliment. It was declared a protected tree in 2003 and, in 2021, the city renamed it for him: Platan profesora Chudoby.

The measurements disagree with each other more than most. Brno's own botanical record puts the girth at 383 centimetres in 2013; the national memorial-tree register gives 475 centimetres for the same trunk. Ninety centimetres is too much to explain by growth alone in that span, so one of the two figures is likely an error rather than a fresh measurement, and this page states both rather than picking a winner. Age is put at roughly 100 to 120 years by different sources, old enough that Chudoba himself would have known it as already substantial when he wrote about it, not as a sapling.

It stands on the corner of Veveří and Pekárenská, wedged into a tight urban plot, growing anyway.

https://botany.cz/cs/platan-na-veveri/ (girth 383cm measured 2013, age approx. 100 years in 2009, declared 2003-01-01)

https://www.em.muni.cz/udalosti/15126-pamatny-platan-nese-jmeno-prvniho-profesora-anglicke-filologie (Masaryk University's own account of the 2022-04-29 renaming ceremony and the Chudoba story, age approx. 120 years)

An earlier pass held this back over an apparent identity conflict between two web sources; resolved this pass with three converging sources (turistika.cz matching the register's 475cm and declaration year exactly, botany.cz's independent 383cm figure at the same corner and declaration date, and Masaryk University's own 2022 renaming-ceremony account naming the same intersection): this is one tree, not two, with a genuine unresolved girth disagreement rather than a case of mistaken identity. Named Platan profesora Chudoby since 2021-12-15 (city environmental department decision), formally renamed at a ceremony 2022-04-29.

trees.name: The Bystrc Lime
trees.age_estimate: past 400 years; estimated at 380 to 400 around the year 2000

location.address: Náměstí 28. dubna, in front of the U Štávů pub, Brno-Bystrc

trees.story:
In 1933 a neighbour tried to smoke a marten out of this tree by packing the hollow with straw and setting it alight.

The lime came through it, and the reason it did is paperwork. Somebody at the heritage office checked and found the tree was already protected, which ended the argument about felling it. It was patched and bound with iron bands instead, and it still wears them.

It is the oldest tree in Brno. About four and a half metres round, fifteen metres tall, standing on the square in Bystrc with the pub tables under it. The trunk is hollow and the original wood is gone. What fills the shell now is a tangle of younger stems and aerial roots the tree grew inside itself, and it still sets seed every year.

The age is an estimate rather than a count, for the obvious reason: 380 to 400 years as of 2000, so somewhere past four centuries now.

When Brno ran its first Tree of the Year contest in 2000, this one won. It went to the national round two years later and came eleventh.

Bystrc was a village long before Brno reached it, and people have been gathering under this tree for as long as anyone wrote it down.
trees.access: Free. On a public square, open at all times. A low iron railing keeps people off the root plate.
trees.transport: Bus 30, 50 or 51 to the Náměstí 28. dubna stop; the tree stands on the square. Roughly 25 minutes from the centre of Brno.

trees.how_to_recognise: A single very broad low crown filling one corner of the square, on a short hollow trunk ringed by an iron fence, with a stone cross beside it and the pub terrace under the branches.
